title: self-hosted-stack-positioning-notes
body:
Context and intent:
This doc is a tactical GTM brief for positioning Redwood Inference against the growing DIY/self-hosted inference stacks centered on vLLM, Text Generation Inference (TGI), and TensorRT-LLM. Audience: sales reps, solutions engineers, product marketing. Goal: concise messaging, objection handling, and an operational checklist for sales conversations where prospects are evaluating build-vs-buy.

Quick thesis (one line):
Teams that prioritize predictable economics, running-time reliability, and enterprise controls tend to prefer a managed inference platform once scale and SLAs matter — the core of our pitch is shifting the decision from "can we run it" to "do we want to own it long term."

Executive summary (bullets):
- Self-hosted stacks (vLLM/TGI/TensorRT) are attractive for early-stage proof-of-concepts: low infra lock-in, maximal control, cheaper at very small scale if you have spare infra and infra expertise.
- Hidden costs emerge quickly: maintenance, kernel tuning, quantization validation, model upgrades, KV cache safety, autoscaling complexity, and production-grade observability.
- Redwood sells against these unknowns: we accept the complexity as our product and deliver predictable per-token economics plus operational guarantees (rollouts, fallbacks, cost control).
- Recommended GTM: emphasize "ops-as-differentiator" not just performance numbers — highlight runbooks, SLOs, and mitigation patterns that DIY teams overlook.

Technical comparison (high-level):
- vLLM: excellent for research/experimentation on CPU/GPU with strong batching semantics. Pros: flexible, strong community. Cons: still needs engineering for KV cache persistence, autoscaler glue, and quantization pipelines.
- TGI (Hugging Face): great model compatibility, plug-and-play for many HF models. Pros: fast on baseline GPU setups, good ecosystem. Cons: operationalizing at multi-tenant scale, deterministic fallbacks, and cost accounting are lacking out-of-the-box.
- TensorRT-LLM: focused on extreme latency/throughput using TensorRT kernels. Pros: best-in-class throughput on supported hardware and quantization formats. Cons: limited model coverage, heavy per-model engineering, brittle on mixed-sequence workloads.

Key operational gaps DIY teams face (these are our battlecards):
1) Model onboarding time: conversions, kernel tuning, and performance validation per model variant.
2) Quantization regressions: numerical deltas and hallucination risk require test harnesses and rollback logic.
3) Autoscaling and cold-starts: continuous batching and KV-cache warm-up to meet p50/p95 SLOs.
4) Cost visibility: token-level breakdowns, customer-specific cost attribution across tenants/routes.
5) Reliability & fallbacks: policy-driven fallback to cheaper variants/regions during capacity constraints.
6) Observability: per-request traces tied to prompt sets and prompt-level evals for regressions.

Concrete examples / short anecdotes for reps:
- Prospect A (startup): had vLLM PoC running on 4 GPUs. When traffic tripled latency SLOs slipped because of cold KV cache and inefficient batching. They underestimated engineering hours to build prefix cache invalidation and this pushed timeline by 6 weeks.
- Prospect B (enterprise): tried TensorRT-LLM to squeeze cost. Ended up rebuilding pipelines for model updates every time a new quantization-friendly checkpoint was released; lacked a rollout framework so production deploys were slow and risky.

Build-vs-buy cost factors to call out in discovery (questions reps should ask):
- Current and projected QPS and peak concurrency? (Batching efficiency scales non-linearly.)
- Do you have existing GPU pool capacity that can be reallocated long-term? (Spare capacity vs committed infra matters.)
- SLA expectations for latency (p50/p95) and uptime (SLA financials)?
- Team composition: do you have 1+ infra engineers who can own inference runtime and on-call 24/7?
- Compliance/hosting constraints: VPC, on-prem, KMS/HSM needs?
- How critical is predictable unit cost vs raw lowest possible spend?

Redwood differentiation: messaging snippets (short):
- "We run the inference stack so your engineers can build product features, not kernel patches."
- "Predictable per-token economics with guardrails — not a surprise bill when usage scales."
- "Enterprise rollouts, not one-off optimizations — canary/A-B and auto-fallback built in."

Objection handling (common DIY objections and responses):
- "We can do it cheaper ourselves." -> Response: "At very small scale maybe, but we see ~3–6x hidden ops cost while reaching production-grade reliability. We can run a pilot and model your TCO over 12 months including SRE time."
- "We need full control of the hardware." -> Response: "We support Dedicated and Private deployments; you get control without rebuilding the operational layer — and we can integrate with on-prem KMS/HSM for compliance."
- "Open-source tooling is good enough for us." -> Response: "Open-source is great for prototyping. The risk is in the last-mile: production operational primitives like safe rollouts, prefix caching semantics, token-level billing, and model-quality regressions. Those are where customers pay us to de-risk their product launches."

Pilot / evaluation checklist (for SEs to run with prospects):
- Baseline: run a 2-week PoC with representative prompts and traffic shape (not synthetic tiny queries).
- Metrics to capture: p50/p95 latency, CPU/GPU utilization, cost per 1M tokens (including infra amortization), failure modes, and tail-latency causes.
- Stress tests: surge to 3x usual QPS and observe autoscaler, cold cache behavior, and fallback policies.
- Model lifecycle test: push a model patch/quantized variant and validate rollout + rollback time and correctness tests.
- Observability validation: ensure traces can answer prompt->response failures and link to eval prompts.

Suggested collateral to attach to outbound / AE decks:
- One-pager: "When to build vs buy: a 6-question decision guide" (sales checklist).
- TCO calculator (spreadsheet): inputs for infra amortization, SRE FTE cost, storage/KV, licensing, and expected QPS.
- Short case study: how a customer reduced incident time-to-detect by 4x after switching to Redwood.

Open questions for product/engineering (for roadmap alignment):
- Which additional telemetry hooks would most shorten a prospect's PoC evaluation time? (prompt-level eval webhooks?)
- Can we publish a standardized "self-host delta" TCO model that maps to common DIY stacks?
- Are there frictionless integrations we can ship with vLLM/TGI to make migration easier while still owning the operational layer?

Action items (next steps):
- PM: produce the 1-pager decision guide (due 2026-03-20).
- SE: draft a 2-week PoC playbook that captures the checklist above (due 2026-03-17).
- Marketing: create a short landing page A/B test targeting "inference ops" keywords emphasizing predictable economics and rollouts.

Notes to self / informal fragments:
- Might be worth capturing a one-slide technical diff showing where engineering hours go for each stack (e.g., model conversion, kernel tuning, autoscaling, QA).
- Consider a short FAQ doc for legal/procurement re: Dedicated and Private options.
- Flag: collect anonymized PoC metrics from CS to quantify median ops overhead for DIY conversions.

References & links:
- Internal: github.com/redwood-inference/poe-profiles (PoC templates)
- Jira: INF-412 (self-host comparisons research ticket)
- External: vLLM repo, Hugging Face TGI docs, NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM blog posts

End of draft.
